Flatten an arbitrarily nested array of integers into one flat list, leaving out nulls.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/flatten-array) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: flatten_array.nomi
//# Flattens a nested array into one list of its values, dropping nulls.

/// One element of a nested array: a value, an array of elements, or null.
pub enum Nested {
    Value Int
    Array List<Nested>
    Null
}

/// Every value in `array`, at any depth, in order; nulls are left out.
pub fn flatten(array: List<Nested>) -> List<Int> {
    array
    |> Iter.flat_map(values)
    |> Iter.to_list()
}

/// The values one element holds.
fn values(element: Nested) -> List<Int> {
    case element {
        .Value(n) -> [n]
        .Array(elements) -> flatten(elements)
        .Null -> []
    }
}

// FILE: flatten_array_test.nomi
import flatten_array.{self, Nested}

test "flatten" {
    cases = [
        #("empty", [], []),
        #("no nesting", [Nested.Value(0), .Value(1), .Value(2)], [0, 1, 2]),
        #("flattens a nested array", [
            .Array([.Array([])]),
        ], []),
        #(
            "flattens array with just integers present",
            [
                .Value(1),
                .Array([.Value(2), .Value(3), .Value(4), .Value(5), .Value(6), .Value(7)]),
                .Value(8),
            ],
            [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8],
        ),
        #("5 level nesting", [
            .Value(0),
            .Value(2),
            .Array([
                .Array([.Value(2), .Value(3)]),
                .Value(8),
                .Value(100),
                .Value(4),
                .Array([
                    .Array([.Array([.Value(50)])]),
                ]),
            ]),
            .Value(-2),
        ], [0, 2, 2, 3, 8, 100, 4, 50, -2]),
        #("6 level nesting", [
            .Value(1),
            .Array([
                .Value(2),
                .Array([.Array([.Value(3)])]),
                .Array([
                    .Value(4),
                    .Array([.Array([.Value(5)])]),
                ]),
                .Value(6),
                .Value(7),
            ]),
            .Value(8),
        ], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]),
        #("null values are omitted from the final result", [.Value(1), .Value(2), .Null], [1, 2]),
        #(
            "consecutive null values at the front of the array are omitted from the final result",
            [.Null, .Null, .Value(3)],
            [3],
        ),
        #(
            "consecutive null values in the middle of the array are omitted from the final result",
            [.Value(1), .Null, .Null, .Value(4)],
            [1, 4],
        ),
        #("6 level nested array with null values", [
            .Value(0),
            .Value(2),
            .Array([
                .Array([.Value(2), .Value(3)]),
                .Value(8),
                .Array([.Array([.Value(100)])]),
                .Null,
                .Array([.Array([.Null])]),
            ]),
            .Value(-2),
        ], [0, 2, 2, 3, 8, 100, -2]),
        #("all values in nested array are null", [
            .Null,
            .Array([
                .Array([.Array([.Null])]),
            ]),
            .Null,
            .Null,
            .Array([.Array([.Null, .Null]), .Null]),
            .Null,
        ], []),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, array, expected), description {
        assert flatten_array.flatten(array) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The input is a recursive enum, `Nested`: a `Value Int`, an `Array List<Nested>`, or `Null`. The canonical arrays mix numbers, arrays and nulls, and the enum names each kind, so `flatten` handles exactly those three and the compiler checks it does.
- `flatten` is `Iter.flat_map` over the top level with `values`, which answers one element's values: `[n]` for a value, the flattened array for an array, and `[]` for a null. The recursion is between the two functions, one call per nested array.
- The canonical arrays are written as `Nested` values in the tests, `[.Value(1), .Array([.Value(2)]), .Null]`. std/json's `Json` could hold them, but it also holds strings, floats and objects, which this input never has, and there is no `Json` typed literal to write them as JSON.
- The table needs no annotation. Its first row's arrays are empty, the second row names the enum, `Nested.Value(0)`, and every variant after it is bare.
- The 11 current canonical cases are one `subtests` table named by the description column. The four cases that newer ones reimplement (the same arrays, described as lists instead of arrays) are left out.
